The student explains this by relating the nesting to the dangling-else rule: the outer if fails, and the else belongs to the inner if, so the else is skipped too. The student does not trace the else-if chain, but the main reasoning about the nested ifs is correct.

rows.text: sum builds a total, count counts.
rows.label: L1
rows.label_why: Names the two roles without relating them to the code's values or purpose.
rows.judge_why: The answer correctly names sum as the accumulator (it builds a total) and count as the counter, but it does not apply this to the code's lines or values and does not contrast the two updates.

rows.text: The cast happens first, so (int) Math.random() is 0 and the die is always 1. Cast after multiplying.
rows.label: L3
rows.label_why: Locates the cause in the given failing test (the cast binds first) and gives the fix.
rows.judge_why: The student finds the cause of this one failing case: the cast binds to Math.random() before the multiplication, so the value is 0 and the die is always 1. They then fix it by moving the cast after the multiplication, and locating and fixing one given failing case is L3.

rows.text: continue jumps to the next i for the even numbers, break stops the loop completely at 5.
rows.label: L3
rows.label_why: Relates continue and break to the passes they affect in this loop.
rows.judge_why: The answer correctly applies continue (the even values of i) and break (i == 5) to this loop's values, but it describes each separately and never relates them to each other.

rows.text: A loop that never stops because its condition stays true.
rows.label: L1
rows.label_why: States the definition of an infinite loop without applying it to this code.
rows.judge_why: The student gives a correct general definition of an infinite loop (its condition stays true, so it never stops) but does not apply it to this code, for example by noting that i += 0.5 leaves the int i at 0.

rows.text: new fills the array with 0s, but a local variable has no value until you give it one.
rows.label: L3
rows.label_why: Relates array default values to local variables that have none.
rows.judge_why: The answer correctly explains why a[0] prints: new gives array elements a default 0, while a local variable has no value until it is assigned. This is the parallel relation between array default values and definite assignment.

rows.text: Something like [I@ and a hex code, not the numbers.
rows.label: L1
rows.label_why: Correct description of what is printed, with no reason.
rows.judge_why: The student gives the correct form of the output ("[I@" plus a hex code, not the elements) but doesn't trace how println turns the reference into text, so this is one correct aspect stated without being applied step by step.

rows.text: for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) a[i] = a[i] * 10;
rows.label: L4
rows.label_why: Writes correct new code that changes the array elements.
run_facts: the student's code runs; after it: a = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] -> [50, 40, 30, 20, 10]; output '5 / 4 / 3 / 2 / 1'
rows.judge_why: The question's code uses a for-each loop that assigns only to the copy x, so the array never changes and the output stays 5 4 3 2 1. The student wrote a correct index traversal that writes each a[i] back, which fixes this one given failing case, and fixing one given case is L3 even though the student gives no explanation.

rows.text: Otherwise a[i] is overwritten before it is saved.
rows.label: L3
rows.label_why: Relates t to the swap: without it a[i] is overwritten before it is saved.
rows.judge_why: The answer explains why the temporary is needed: the assignment a[i] = a[r] overwrites a[i], so its old value must be saved first. This ties the order of assignments to the exchange, but it does not go on to describe the broken swap or the class of inputs where it fails.

rows.text: It is a table to look up a month name from its number.
rows.label: L1
rows.label_why: Names the element (a lookup table) without applying it to the code's values.
rows.judge_why: In one correct sentence the student says what the months array is for: a table that turns a month number into its name. This matches what months[m - 1] does, printing Mar for m = 3.

rows.text: It marks whether k is not prime; everything starts as false.
rows.label: L1
rows.label_why: States what composite[k] means and its default, without applying it to the sieve.
rows.judge_why: Both facts are right: composite[k] flags that k is not prime, and every flag starts as false. But they are two separate statements that the answer never applies to this code's values or connects to how the sieve works.

rows.text: No, b times a is 3 4 / 1 2, so the order matters.
rows.label: L4
rows.label_why: Computes the changed product b × a and concludes correctly that the order matters.
rows.judge_why: The student correctly works out the swapped product b×a as {{3,4},{1,2}}, which differs from c = {{2,1},{4,3}}, and concludes that order matters; this is a value result for changed code without reasoning about what is conserved, so it is L2, not L4.

rows.text: 42, an empty string, and "Ann Lee".
rows.label: L1
rows.label_why: Correct values with no justification.
run_facts: confirmed by the run: age = 42 (final); rest = "" (final); name = "Ann Lee" (final)
rows.judge_why: The student gives the right three values (42, "", "Ann Lee") but doesn't explain why readLine returns an empty string after readInt, so this is a bare correct result, which is L1.

rows.text: readInt takes 42 but not the Enter, so readLine just finishes that line.
rows.label: L3
rows.label_why: Relates readInt and readLine: readInt leaves the end of the line, which readLine returns.
rows.judge_why: The student says readInt consumes 42 and leaves the Enter, so the next readLine only finishes that same line. That is a correct causal link between the token read and the line read through their shared input position, and it explains why rest is empty without tracing the code value by value.

rows.text: No, the user decides each time, while it is running.
rows.label: L4
rows.label_why: Reasons correctly about a program that is not the given code: interactive input decides the rounds while it runs.
rows.judge_why: The answer says the number of rounds can't be known ahead of time because the user decides while the program runs. That ties each reply to whether the loop goes on, which is the correct right-rule against InputFixedBeforeRun, linked to the loop's control flow.

rows.text: It reads from standard input and writes to standard output.
rows.label: L1
rows.label_why: States the definition of a filter.
rows.judge_why: The student gives the general definition of a filter (it reads standard input and writes standard output) but never applies it to this code: nothing about the non-negative test, the read loop or the pipeline is mentioned.

rows.text: The circles are never erased, so you get a trail.
rows.label: L4
rows.label_why: Correctly predicts the effect of removing clear(): earlier circles stay, leaving a trail.
rows.judge_why: The question asks about code that has been changed: StdDraw.clear() is removed. The student gives the reason (circles are no longer erased) and correctly predicts the effect (a trail builds up), which is the change-prediction way of animation at L4.

rows.text: You need System.exit(0) at the end of main.
rows.label: L3
rows.label_why: Locates the fix for the given failing case (System.exit(0) at the end of main).
rows.judge_why: The student gives the right fix for this one hanging program (end main with System.exit(0)) but does not explain why the terminal hangs or name the general class of programs that hang, so by the boundary rule this is L3, not L4.

rows.text: Page 2, it links nowhere.
rows.label: L1
rows.label_why: Names the dangling page with the defining fact.
rows.judge_why: The student uses the graph's values to pick out the correct page (page 2) and gives a short reason (it has no outgoing links), so this is the dangling-page definition applied to this code. That is L2, not just stating the rule (L1).

rows.text: The surfer gets trapped in that group and the other pages get rank 0.
rows.label: L4
rows.label_why: Correctly predicts the effect of removing teleportation: the surfer is trapped and other pages get rank 0.
rows.judge_why: The student reasons about code that has been changed (the random jump removed). They say correctly that a closed group of pages traps the surfer and that every other page gets rank 0, which means the chain no longer mixes.

rows.text: a and b are 5 and total is 11.5; after the last line total is still 11.5, because it already has a value.
rows.label: L0
rows.label_why: Applies a wrong rule: an assignment replaces the old value, so total becomes about 12.42.
run_facts: stated total = 11.5 (final); the code gives total = 12.42
rows.judge_why: The student traces a, b and the first total correctly, but then says the last assignment leaves total at 11.5 'because it already has a value'; this is the static-variable rule, which contradicts Java (total becomes 12.42).

rows.text: int c; declares c, so c is 0.
rows.label: L0
rows.label_why: Applies a wrong rule: a local variable has no default value, so c cannot be read.
rows.judge_why: The student says that declaring the local variable c gives it the value 0, but in Java a local variable has no value until it is assigned, so c + 1 does not compile.

rows.text: After t = a and a = b, a is b. Then b = t means b equals a, so both are b.
rows.label: L0
rows.label_why: Switches rules within one trace: b = t is read as "b equals a", not as storing t's old value.
rows.judge_why: The student says t holds the variable a itself rather than the value a had when t = a ran, so they conclude both variables end up as b and miss that the three lines swap a and b.

rows.text: You could write b as !(5 < n < 10).
rows.label: L0
rows.label_why: Uses a maths-style chained comparison, which is not valid Java.
rows.judge_why: The student rewrites b as the maths-style range !(5 < n < 10), which does not compile in Java, and keeps the !( ) instead of applying De Morgan, so the answer uses a rule that goes against Java.

rows.text: isDone = (i % 5 == 0); would do the same as the if.
rows.label: L1
rows.label_why: The claim happens to be right for this loop, but no reason is given (in general a flag must stay set once found).
rows.judge_why: The answer skips the output and the stop condition the question asks for. It only claims, with no reason given, that storing the condition directly in isDone would do the same as the if. That claim is correct for this code but is a familiar rewrite with no stated reasoning, so it is graded as a relation within the given code (L3), not L4.

rows.text: System.out.println("x is 5"); sets x to 5.
rows.label: L0
rows.label_why: Everyday reading: printing text does not assign a value to x.
run_facts: stated x = 5 (final); the code has no variable x, so nothing sets it
rows.judge_why: The student treats printed text as if it acted on the program: they say println("x is 5") sets x to 5. That is the documented everyday misreading of output, and it ignores the actual print/println output of the given code.

rows.text: Add v to sum first, then check if it was negative and subtract it again.
rows.label: L0
rows.label_why: Checks the value after using it; count would still include -2, so the average changes.
rows.judge_why: The answer does not say what is printed for either input; instead it proposes adding v to sum and then subtracting it back if v is negative, which correctly describes one part of the accumulator update but is not applied to the values, does not mention count or the sentinel, and does not reach the output 5.0 or the empty output when the first value is 99999.

rows.text: The square uses 0.5 as the centre, but the point uses pixels, so both are in the middle.
rows.label: L0
rows.label_why: Uses two scales at once: StdDraw uses the unit square for every command.
rows.judge_why: The student claims point(256, 256) is in the middle because it 'uses pixels'. That is the documented PixelCoordinates misconception: in the default unit square, (256, 256) is far outside the visible canvas.

rows.text: Writing 3.14159 in the formula is just as clear as a name.
rows.label: L0
rows.label_why: Applies a wrong style rule: an unnamed 3.14159 hides its meaning.
rows.judge_why: The answer says a literal 3.14159 in the formula is as clear as a name, which is the MagicNumbers wrong rule, and it never considers the loop's 0 and 1, which are not magic numbers.

rows.text: Braces are pointless, I never write them.
rows.label: L0
rows.label_why: Applies a wrong style rule; leaving braces out is legal but invites errors.
rows.judge_why: The answer calls braces pointless and says the student never writes them, which matches the MissingBraces misconception; it contradicts the rule that only braces group several statements into one body.

rows.text: Every expression must be fully in parentheses, otherwise Java guesses the order.
rows.label: L0
rows.label_why: Contradicts Java: precedence is fixed, Java never guesses the order.
rows.judge_why: The student says Java 'guesses the order' without parentheses, but Java has fixed precedence rules: * binds tighter than +, so the code compiles and r = 1 + (2 * 3) = 7. The student's rule contradicts Java, and the answer never gives r.

rows.text: Indentation does not matter, I indent however I like.
rows.label: L0
rows.label_why: Treats indentation as unimportant for readers, and gives no output; misleading indentation is the problem here.
rows.judge_why: The student states one correct rule (the compiler ignores indentation) but does not apply it to this code: they don't say that only the first println belongs to the braceless if, and they don't predict the output for score = 50.

rows.text: I can rename the file to Greeting.java and keep public class hello.
rows.label: L0
rows.label_why: Applies a wrong rule: a public class must be in a file with its name.
rows.judge_why: The student says the file can be renamed to Greeting.java while keeping public class hello, so they treat the file name and the public class name as independent, which contradicts Java's rule that public class hello must be saved in hello.java.

rows.text: For a 3 × 3 board I would use a[0].length, but for any 2-D array I need a[i].length.
rows.label: L4
rows.label_why: States the class of inputs (rows of different lengths) for which a[0].length fails.
rows.judge_why: The student correctly says that a general printing method must bound each row by a[i].length rather than a[0].length, but never says why (that rows can have different lengths) and gives no loop or trace, so this is one correct rule stated without being applied.

rows.text: System.out.println(count + 1) shows one more, but count + 1 on its own line does not change count.
rows.label: L3
rows.label_why: Relates the same expression used as a value and as a statement.
rows.judge_why: The answer gives none of the three requested statements (count = count + 1; count += 1; count++;) and offers only one correct point: printing or evaluating count + 1 does not change count.

rows.text: When i is 3 it prints 1 2 3.
rows.label: L1
rows.label_why: Covers one pass (i = 3) with its values; the other rows and the purpose are missing.
rows.judge_why: The answer correctly gives one row (the last outer pass, i = 3) but not the full output, and it does not explain how the two loops work together across all passes.

rows.text: if (value == 1) result = 30; elif (value == 2 || value == 3) result = -10; else result = 5;
rows.label: L0
rows.label_why: Uses elif, which Java does not have; the new code does not compile.
run_facts: stated result = 5 (final); the code gives result = 30
stated result = -10 (final); the code gives result = 30
rows.judge_why: The student turns the switch into an equivalent else-if chain, deduced from the code: case 1 becomes the first test, the case 2 to case 3 fall-through becomes one || condition, and default becomes the final else; the branch logic is correct, but 'elif' is Python, not Java, so the code would not compile.

rows.text: B C A D E: sum has to start at 0 before the loop, be added to in every pass, and be printed once after the loop.
rows.label: L3
rows.label_why: Orders the lines and relates each one to its role in the accumulator plan.
rows.judge_why: The order B C A D E is correct, and the student explains it by tying each accumulator statement to where it sits around the loop: start at 0 before it, add on every pass, print once after it. That relates the accumulator to the loop body, which is the relational (L3) way, not a line-by-line trace.
